sheets.title: A conductor decides the field before you calculate
sheets.sub: Every conductor fact comes from one sentence: free charges move until they stop moving.

blocks.s: A metal has free electrons. If anything pushes them, they move. Equilibrium means they have stopped, so nothing is pushing them.

blocks.t: why the field inside is zero
lines: If $E$ were non-zero inside, a free electron would feel $eE$ and move. It has stopped, so $E_{\mathrm{inside}}=0$.

blocks.t: why the field must be perpendicular to the surface
lines: On the surface the potential is constant. Along the surface $dV=0$, and $dV=-\vec E\cdot d\vec l$ for every such $d\vec l$: only the normal component survives.

blocks.t: how large the surface field is (pillbox)
lines: Take a thin pillbox straddling the surface, face area $A$, only the outside face is in a field: $EA=\sigma A/\varepsilon_0$.
$\Rightarrow\ E_{\mathrm{surface}}=\sigma/\varepsilon_0$
$E_{\mathrm{inside}}=0$;  the whole conductor, cavity walls included, is one potential
just outside: $E=\sigma/\varepsilon_0$, perpendicular to the metal
a cavity holding $+q$ shows $-q$ on its wall and $+q$ on the outer surface
an empty cavity is shielded from fields outside it

blocks.s: $E=0$ is not $V=0$. A charged shell has no field inside and still sits at $V=kQ/R$: zero slope, non-zero height.

blocks.t: induced charge, from one Gaussian surface
lines: Draw any closed surface inside the metal. Every point on it has $E=0$, so $\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A=0$.
The enclosed charge must then be zero: the wall carries $-q$, and since the conductor is neutral, $+q$ appears outside.
The outer surface knows only the total charge, not where it is hidden - so a cavity is shielded.

blocks.s: Name a surface where $|\vec E|$ is constant and $\vec E$ is parallel or perpendicular to $d\vec A$, then use $\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A=Q_{\mathrm{enc}}/\varepsilon_0$.
The flux integral is only useful after symmetry has turned it into $E$ times an area. Otherwise Gauss is still true, just not calculable.

lines: Radius $10\ \mathrm{cm}$, charge $1\ \mu\mathrm{C}$: $V_s=9.0\times10^4\ \mathrm{V}$, $E_s=9.0\times10^5\ \mathrm{V/m}$; both fall off outside as $1/r$ and $1/r^2$.

blocks.s: One charged plate gives $\sigma/2\varepsilon_0$, but a capacitor gap gives $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$ - two plates, two contributions.

items.cap: A neutral shell with $+q$ in the cavity: $-q$ on the wall, $+q$ outside, $E=0$ in the metal.
Field is flat and non-zero inside; the step in $V$ at $r=R$ marks where the charge sits.

blocks.s: Say where the charge sits, then what the potential is. Neither step needs a capacitor formula.

sheets.title: Capacitance: the plate formula and the one slab rule
sheets.sub: Capacitance is charge needed per volt. Derive it once for plates, then a single rule covers dielectric, metal and vacuum.

blocks.t: Why C depends on geometry alone
the ratio is fixed by shape and medium
lines: Every field and potential is proportional to the charges that produce it. Double every $q$ and every $V$ doubles.
So $Q/V$ cannot depend on $Q$. What is left is geometry and the medium: $C=\varepsilon_0 A/d$ for plates, $4\pi\varepsilon_0R$ for an isolated sphere.

blocks.s: A capacitor holds $+Q$ and $-Q$, so its net charge is zero. "Charge on the capacitor" always means the positive plate.

blocks.t: The plate formula, derived in three lines

lines: Gap field of two opposite plates: $E=\dfrac{Q/2}{\varepsilon_0A}+\dfrac{Q/2}{\varepsilon_0A}=\dfrac{Q}{\varepsilon_0A}$ (the two plates add).
Voltage between them: $V=Ed=\dfrac{Qd}{\varepsilon_0A}$.
Divide: $C=\dfrac{Q}{V}=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d}$, and with a dielectric filling the gap $C=\dfrac{K\varepsilon_0A}{d}$.
$C=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d}$,  $\ C=\dfrac{K\varepsilon_0A}{d}$;  $\varepsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F/m}$, $4\pi\varepsilon_0=1.11\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{F/m}$
Area $100\ \mathrm{cm^2}$, gap $1\ \mathrm{mm}$: air $88.5\ \mathrm{pF}$; with $K=5$, $443\ \mathrm{pF}$. Doubling the gap halves $C$; an isolated $1\ \mathrm{cm}$ sphere is only $1.1\ \mathrm{pF}$.

blocks.t: One slab rule for every gap

lines: With a slab of thickness $t$ and constant free charge: $E_{\mathrm{vac}}=\dfrac{Q}{\varepsilon_0A}$, $E_{\mathrm{slab}}=\dfrac{Q}{K\varepsilon_0A}$.
Add the two voltage drops: $V=E_{\mathrm{vac}}(d-t)+E_{\mathrm{slab}}\,t=\dfrac{Q}{\varepsilon_0A}\left(d-t+\dfrac{t}{K}\right)$.
Divide by $Q$: $C=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d-t+t/K}$. Metal is the limit $K\to\infty$, giving $C=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d-t}$ - the thickness is simply removed.

blocks.t: use it in all three cases
lines: dielectric slab: $C=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d-t+t/K}$;  metal slab: $C=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d-t}$;  vacuum: $C=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d}$
two layers: $\dfrac{1}{C}=\dfrac{t_1}{K_1\varepsilon_0A}+\dfrac{t_2}{K_2\varepsilon_0A}$;  only total thickness of each layer matters

blocks.s: Use the overlap area, never the sum of both plate areas. And $C=\varepsilon_0A/d$ needs $d$ small compared with the plate width; edge fringing always adds a little.

blocks.t: Many plates, and plates with unequal charge
n plates and two odd charges
lines: Interleave $n$ plates, alternate ones wired to the two terminals: there are $n-1$ gaps, all at the same voltage, so $C=(n-1)\varepsilon_0A/d$.
Large plates carrying $Q_1,Q_2$: the facing surfaces hold $\pm(Q_1-Q_2)/2$, since only that much can be shared across the gap.
Then $V_1-V_2=\dfrac{(Q_1-Q_2)d}{2\varepsilon_0A}$. A net plate charge is not the same as the facing charge.

items.cap: A floating metal slab removes its own thickness from the voltage drop.

blocks.s: $C$ is geometry plus medium. Derive the plate formula once, then replace the filled thickness by $t/K$.

sheets.title: Sphere, cylinder and connected conductors
sheets.sub: One method: assign the charge, find E by Gauss, integrate to get V, divide. The geometry only changes the integral.

blocks.t: Potential inside, and why the graph is flat

lines: Outside, $V(r)=-\int_\infty^r kQ/r'^2\,dr'=kQ/r$.
Inside, the path in from the surface costs nothing because $E=0$, so $V=kQ/R$ all the way in. The graph steps at $r=R$ because that is where the charge sits, not because $V$ jumps.
Gauss between the spheres: $E=\dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2}$, independent of the outer shell.
Integrate from $a$ to $b$: $V=\dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\dfrac{1}{a}-\dfrac{1}{b}\right)$.
Divide: $C=4\pi\varepsilon_0\dfrac{ab}{b-a}$.  Let $b\to\infty$: the isolated sphere $4\pi\varepsilon_0a$.
Let $b-a\ll a$: the area is $4\pi a^2$ and the plate formula returns - always check a new geometry against that limit.
Gauss on a cylinder of radius $r$ and length $L$: $E\cdot2\pi rL=\dfrac{\lambda L}{\varepsilon_0}$, so $E=\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0r}$.
Integrate $1/r$: $V=\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\ln\dfrac{b}{a}$, hence $C=\dfrac{2\pi\varepsilon_0L}{\ln(b/a)}$.
Radial layers in series add their logs: $\dfrac{1}{C/L}=\sum_i\dfrac{\ln(r_{i+1}/r_i)}{2\pi\varepsilon_i}$.

blocks.t: Two connected spheres: potential is shared, charge is not
why the smaller sphere wins the field
lines: A wire makes one conductor, so $V_a=V_b$: $\dfrac{Q_a}{a}=\dfrac{Q_b}{b}\Rightarrow Q_a=Q\dfrac{a}{a+b}$.
Surface fields: $E=kQ_a/a^2$ and $E=kQ_b/b^2$, so $\dfrac{E_a}{E_b}=\dfrac{b}{a}$ - the smaller sphere has the larger field.
That is why a pointed conductor sparks first.

blocks.s: These distant-sphere results need separation $\gg$ radius. For nearby spheres the induced charge makes the surface distribution non-uniform and $V$ is no longer $kQ/r$.

lines: two distant spheres, radii $a,b$, opposite charges: $C\simeq4\pi\varepsilon_0\dfrac{ab}{a+b}$ (this is the series combination $1/C=1/C_a+1/C_b$)
sphere of radius $a$ coated to radius $b$ with dielectric $K$: $\dfrac{1}{C}=\dfrac{(1/a-1/b)/K+1/b}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$ - add the dielectric drop to the vacuum drop
Coax with $a=2\ \mathrm{mm}$, $b=10\ \mathrm{mm}$, $L=1\ \mathrm{m}$: $C=2\pi\varepsilon_0/\ln5=77\ \mathrm{pF}$; the same cable in oil of $K=2.2$ gives $170\ \mathrm{pF}$.
Two spheres $1\ \mathrm{cm}$ and $4\ \mathrm{cm}$ sharing $100\ \mu\mathrm{C}$: the small one takes $20\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ but has $16\times$ the surface field of the large one.

items.cap: Concentric spheres: $E\propto1/r^2$, and only the part between $a$ and $b$ sets $V$.
Coaxial cylinders: $E\propto1/r$, so the voltage brings a logarithm.

blocks.s: Assign $Q$, get $E$ from Gauss, integrate to $V$, divide. Check every new geometry against the plate limit.

sheets.title: Networks: islands, bridges, ladders
sheets.sub: Wires make islands. Charge is conserved on each island, not on each capacitor - derive every combination from that.

lines: Two capacitors in a line make the middle island. If it started neutral it stays neutral, so both carry the same $Q$.
The voltages add: $V=\dfrac{Q}{C_1}+\dfrac{Q}{C_2}$, so $\dfrac{1}{C_{\mathrm{eq}}}=\dfrac{1}{C_1}+\dfrac{1}{C_2}$.
The smallest capacitor then takes the largest share of the voltage.
Both are across the same two nodes, so $V$ is common and the charges add: $Q=C_1V+C_2V$.
$\Rightarrow C_{\mathrm{eq}}=C_1+C_2$. Energy follows: series $\dfrac{U_i}{U}=\dfrac{C_{\mathrm{eq}}}{C_i}$, parallel $\dfrac{U_i}{U}=\dfrac{C_i}{C_{\mathrm{eq}}}$.

blocks.s: Series or parallel is decided by the wires, not by the drawing - redraw first. A precharged middle island also breaks the equal-charge rule.

blocks.t: The island method that never fails

lines: Each floating island has a fixed net charge $Q_i^{\mathrm{init}}$. Every plate on it holds $C(V_i-V_j)$ against a neighbour.
Add them with signs: $\sum_j C_{ij}(V_i-V_j)=Q_i^{\mathrm{init}}$. One equation per floating island.
Solve for the potentials, then read each capacitor as $q=C\,\Delta V$.

blocks.s: Island types: grounded $\Rightarrow V=0$; battery-connected $\Rightarrow$ difference fixed; floating $\Rightarrow$ net charge fixed.

lines: Each arm divides the same applied voltage: $V_X=V\dfrac{C_1}{C_1+C_2}$ and $V_Y=V\dfrac{C_3}{C_3+C_4}$.
It carries nothing when $V_X=V_Y$, i.e. $\dfrac{C_1}{C_2}=\dfrac{C_3}{C_4}$; otherwise write two island equations.
One more repeat unit must change nothing: the remainder $X$ is in series with $C$, then in parallel with $C$.
$X=C+\dfrac{CX}{C+X}\Rightarrow X=\dfrac{\sqrt5-1}{2}C$ (the negative root is rejected: $C>0$).
cube of twelve equal $C$: opposite vertices $\dfrac{6C}{5}$, edge $\dfrac{12C}{7}$, face diagonal $\dfrac{4C}{3}$
star-delta with $S=ab+bc+ca$: arms $x=S/b$, $y=S/c$, $z=S/a$;  back again $C_{12}=xy/(x+y+z)$

blocks.s: Do not copy the resistor star-delta across: for capacitors the star arm is a sum of products divided by one branch.

lines: $6\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ and $3\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ in series give $2\ \mu\mathrm{F}$; with $4\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ in parallel, $C_{\mathrm{eq}}=6\ \mu\mathrm{F}$. At $12\ \mathrm{V}$: $Q=72\ \mu\mathrm{C}$, $U=432\ \mu\mathrm{J}$.
Audit: the series pair holds $24\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ at $4\ \mathrm{V}$ and $8\ \mathrm{V}$, the $4\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ holds $48\ \mu\mathrm{C}$; and $24+48=72$.

blocks.s: Cut the circuit with a surface crossed by that wire only. The charge that crossed equals the change in enclosed plate charge, signs included - it is not $C\Delta V$ in general.

items.cap: The middle island is what forces series charges to be equal.
Balanced means $V_X=V_Y$: delete the bridge, or write one island equation at each node.

blocks.s: Name the terminals, mark the islands, write one charge equation per island. Folding is a shortcut that must be justified.

sheets.title: Energy, the battery, and the heat bill
sheets.sub: Every energy result is an integral or a ledger. The half comes from the triangle, and the battery is part of the accounting.

lines: Push a small charge $dq$ in while the voltage is $V=q/C$: the work is $dU=V\,dq=\dfrac{q}{C}dq$.
Integrate from $0$ to $Q$: $U=\dfrac{Q^2}{2C}=\dfrac12QV=\dfrac12CV^2$.
On a $V$-$q$ graph this is the area of a triangle, not a rectangle - that is the missing half.
For a parallel plate: $U=\dfrac12CV^2=\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d}\cdot(Ed)^2=\dfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2\,(Ad)$.
Divide by the volume $Ad$: $u=\dfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2$ per unit volume, wherever the field is.

blocks.t: the check that catches sign errors
lines: $2\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ at $100\ \mathrm{V}$: $Q=200\ \mu\mathrm{C}$, $U=0.1\ \mathrm{J}$. Pull the plates to twice the gap with the battery off: $C$ halves, $Q$ stays, so $V$ and $U$ double - you supplied that work.

blocks.t: The one fork: fixed Q or fixed V

lines: At fixed $Q$: $C\to KC$ and $Q$ cannot change, so $V=Q/C$ falls by $K$ and $U=Q^2/2C$ falls by $K$. Energy leaves into the mechanical work.
At fixed $V$: $V$ is pinned, so $Q=CV$ grows by $K$ and $U=\frac12CV^2$ grows by $K$. The cell supplies both the extra energy and the mechanical work.

$1\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ at $100\ \mathrm{V}$, then $K=2$ fills the gap. Battery on: $C$ becomes $2\ \mu\mathrm{F}$, the cell supplies $V^2\Delta C=10\ \mathrm{mJ}$, $U$ rises by $5\ \mathrm{mJ}$, and the other $5\ \mathrm{mJ}$ goes into pulling the slab in.
Battery off: $Q=100\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ is fixed, so $V$ drops to $50\ \mathrm{V}$ and $U$ falls from $5\ \mathrm{mJ}$ to $2.5\ \mathrm{mJ}$ - that released energy is the work the field does on the slab.

blocks.s: Battery work is not field energy. The cell supplies $V^2\Delta C$ while $U$ rises by only $\frac12V^2\Delta C$; differentiating $U$ alone gives the wrong sign for the force.

blocks.t: The heat bill when two capacitors are joined

lines: Islands conserve charge: $C_1V_1+C_2V_2=(C_1+C_2)V_f$, so $V_f=\dfrac{C_1V_1+C_2V_2}{C_1+C_2}$.
Energy before minus after: $H=\dfrac{C_1C_2}{2(C_1+C_2)}(V_1-V_2)^2$ - never negative, and independent of the resistance.
$C_1=2\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ at $100\ \mathrm{V}$, $C_2=3\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ uncharged: $V_f=40\ \mathrm{V}$ and $H=\frac12\cdot\frac65\ \mu\mathrm{F}\cdot100^2=6\ \mathrm{mJ}$.
Check: $10\ \mathrm{mJ}$ before, $4\ \mathrm{mJ}$ after - the missing $6\ \mathrm{mJ}$ is heat. Charging an empty $C$ from a cell loses exactly half of $CE^2$.

items.cap: Work is the area under the $V$-$q$ line: a triangle, hence $\frac12$.
Ask what is held fixed before differentiating. It is the whole chapter in one picture.

blocks.s: Fixed $Q$: differentiate $U$. Fixed $V$: differentiate $U-QV$. Heat: conserve charge, then subtract energies.

sheets.title: Force on plates and dielectrics, from energy
sheets.sub: Write C(x), state the constraint, differentiate. The factor one-half is the thing examiners test.
sheets.source: Capacitors.md ch.5, plus the image method

blocks.t: Force from energy, and the pressure of a charged sphere

lines: At fixed $Q$: $F=-\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{Q^2}{2C}\right)=\dfrac{Q^2}{2C^2}\dfrac{dC}{dx}$.
At fixed $V$ the battery must be included, $\Pi=U-QV=-\frac12CV^2$, so $F=-\dfrac{d\Pi}{dx}=\dfrac12V^2\dfrac{dC}{dx}$.
Same state $Q=CV$ gives the same force either way - the constraint only decides what happens next.

blocks.t: outward pressure on a charged sphere
lines: Expand the radius by $dR$ at fixed $Q$: $U=\dfrac{Q^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0R}$ falls, and $dU=-p\,4\pi R^2dR$.
$\Rightarrow p=\dfrac{Q^2}{32\pi^2\varepsilon_0R^4}$, pushing outward; the net force on the sphere is still zero by symmetry.
$100\ \mathrm{cm^2}$ at $1\ \mathrm{mm}$, $100\ \mathrm{V}$: $p=\frac12\varepsilon_0E^2=0.044\ \mathrm{Pa}$, $F=4.4\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{N}$.
Halve the gap at fixed $Q$: $E$ is unchanged, so $F$ is unchanged. At fixed $V$: $E$ doubles, $F$ quadruples.

blocks.t: why it is half the gap field
lines: A plate does not pull on itself. The field at one plate due to the other is $\dfrac{Q}{2\varepsilon_0A}$ - half the gap field.
So $F=Q\cdot\dfrac{Q}{2\varepsilon_0A}=\dfrac{Q^2}{2\varepsilon_0A}$;  as a pressure, $p=\dfrac{\sigma^2}{2\varepsilon_0}$.
The same answer from energy: $F=-\dfrac{dU}{dx}$ with $U=\dfrac{Q^2x}{2\varepsilon_0A}$ gives $F=-\dfrac{Q^2}{2\varepsilon_0A}$, inward.

blocks.s: Do not write $F=QE$ with the full gap field $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$; the correct force is $QE/2$. That half is the whole question.

blocks.t: A dielectric is always pulled inward

lines: Filled and empty parts are in parallel: $C(x)=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0w}{d}\left[L+(K-1)x\right]$, so $\dfrac{dC}{dx}=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0(K-1)w}{d}$.
At fixed $V$: $F=\dfrac12V^2\dfrac{dC}{dx}=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0(K-1)w}{2d}V^2$, constant, pulling the slab in.
At fixed $Q$: use $V=Q/C(x)$, so $F=\dfrac{Q^2}{2C^2}\dfrac{dC}{dx}$ - same direction, smaller as the slab goes deeper.
Electric force per unit plate width $=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0(K-1)V^2}{2d}$; weight of the raised column per width $=\rho gdh$.
Balance: $h=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0(K-1)V^2}{2\rho gd^2}$ - linear in $K-1$, quadratic in $V$, falling fast as the gap opens.
plate: $F=\dfrac{Q^2}{2\varepsilon_0A}=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0AV^2}{2d^2}$;  slab: $\dfrac{\varepsilon_0(K-1)w}{2d}V^2$;  liquid: $h=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0(K-1)V^2}{2\rho gd^2}$
all three point toward larger $C$ - the one thing that never changes

items.cap: Filled and empty parts are parallel capacitors, so $dC/dx>0$: the slab is dragged in.
The same force lifts a liquid: electric work pays for the rise in gravitational energy.

blocks.s: Write $C(x)$, name the constraint, differentiate the right energy. Force always points toward larger $C$.

sheets.title: Image charge, and a plate that snaps down
sheets.sub: Two questions that look hard and are one construction each: a mirror charge, and an equilibrium that stops existing.

blocks.t: Image charge: the one extension worth keeping

blocks.s: A grounded plane is an equipotential, and two opposite charges of equal size make a whole plane equipotential - so the plane can be replaced by the second charge.

lines: Replace the plane by $-q$ at depth $h$. The real charge is then $2h$ from its image: $F=\dfrac{q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0(2h)^2}=\dfrac{q^2}{16\pi\varepsilon_0h^2}$.
Bringing the charge in from infinity: $W=\dfrac12q\,(V_{\mathrm{image}})=\dfrac{q^2}{16\pi\varepsilon_0h}$ - the half is because the induced charge builds up as you approach.
The plane carries induced charge $-q$, spread with $\sigma(\rho)=-\dfrac{qh}{2\pi(\rho^2+h^2)^{3/2}}$, largest directly below the charge.

blocks.s: Using $q^2/8\pi\varepsilon_0h$ double counts the work of building the induced charge. The energy is half of $q\times$ the image potential, not of $q\times$ the full pair energy.

Why a mirror charge is allowed at all: in the region above the plane, solving Laplace with the plane at $V=0$ gives a unique field. The pair of charges already satisfies that boundary condition, so it must be the right field. Above the plane nobody can tell the difference; below it there is no field to speak of, and the metal is not the image.

blocks.t: image results for a grounded plane
lines: force $\dfrac{q^2}{16\pi\varepsilon_0h^2}$,  work to bring from infinity $\dfrac{q^2}{16\pi\varepsilon_0h}$,  induced charge $-q$
surface density $\sigma(\rho)=-\dfrac{qh}{2\pi(\rho^2+h^2)^{3/2}}$: sharpest directly under the charge, and it integrates to $-q$
grounded sphere of radius $a$ (optional, one line): image $q'=-qa/d$ at $a^2/d$; an isolated neutral sphere needs a second image $+qa/d$ at the centre

blocks.t: Stretch: a plate held on a spring
equilibrium, and where it breaks down
lines: The gap is $d-x$ and the spring pulls back with $kx$, so $kx=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0AV^2}{2(d-x)^2}$. Write $y=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0AV^2}{2kd^2}$ and solve $x(1-x/d)^2=yd$.
The two roots merge when the derivative vanishes too: $x=d/3$, at $V^2=\dfrac{8kd^3}{27\varepsilon_0A}$. Beyond it no equilibrium exists and the plate snaps down.
At fixed charge the force $Q^2/2\varepsilon_0A$ does not depend on $x$, so there is no fold and no snap-down.

blocks.t: Stretch: a plate held on a spring
equilibrium, and where it breaks down
lines: The gap is $d-x$ and the spring pulls back with $kx$, so $kx=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0AV^2}{2(d-x)^2}$. Write $y=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0AV^2}{2kd^2}$ and solve $x(1-x/d)^2=yd$.
The two roots merge when the derivative vanishes too: $x=d/3$, at $V^2=\dfrac{8kd^3}{27\varepsilon_0A}$. Beyond it no equilibrium exists and the plate snaps down.
At fixed charge the force $Q^2/2\varepsilon_0A$ does not depend on $x$, so there is no fold and no snap-down.
$q=1\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ at $h=1\ \mathrm{cm}$ above a grounded plane: $F=0.225\ \mathrm{N}$ and the work to bring it from infinity is $0.45\ \mathrm{mJ}$.
At $2\ \mathrm{cm}$ the force is four times smaller and the energy half: both scale as $1/h^2$ and $1/h$, so the energy is always the force times $h/2$.

items.cap: The image makes the plane equipotential; real-image separation is $2h$, not $h$.
Two equilibria appear, then merge and disappear: that is the snap-down.

blocks.s: Mirror the charge to make the boundary equipotential, then treat it as a real Coulomb problem - but count energy once, not twice.

sheets.title: Dielectrics: why the field falls, and layers vs patches
sheets.sub: Polarisation puts bound charge on the faces. Whether the field falls is decided by the constraint, not by the material alone.

blocks.t: why E falls by K at fixed free charge
lines: The applied field lines up molecular dipoles; their bound charge appears on the faces, opposing the free charge.

The net field inside is the free field minus the bound contribution: $E=\dfrac{\sigma_{\mathrm{free}}-\sigma_b}{\varepsilon_0}=\dfrac{\sigma_{\mathrm{free}}}{K\varepsilon_0}$, using $\sigma_b=\sigma_{\mathrm{free}}\left(1-\dfrac1K\right)$.
That is the whole of "the dielectric reduces the field": it happens because the bound charge is there, not because the material absorbs field.

blocks.t: why nothing falls with the battery on
lines: The cell holds the plates at fixed $V$, so $E=V/d$ cannot change. Instead it pushes in more free charge until $Q=KQ_0$.
Capacitance rises by $K$ either way - it is the charge, not the field, that does the extra work.
fixed $Q$: $E=\dfrac{E_0}{K}$, $V=\dfrac{V_0}{K}$, $C=KC_0$, $U=\dfrac{U_0}{K}$  |  fixed $V$: $E=E_0$, $C=KC_0$, $Q=KQ_0$, $U=KU_0$

blocks.s: "A dielectric always reduces the field" is false. Fill the gap with the battery still connected and $E$ is untouched - the charge grows instead.

lines: No free charge at the interface, so the same $D=Q/A$ crosses both layers: $E_i=\dfrac{Q}{K_i\varepsilon_0A}$.
Voltages add: $V=\sum\dfrac{Q\,t_i}{K_i\varepsilon_0A}\Rightarrow\dfrac{1}{C}=\sum\dfrac{t_i}{K_i\varepsilon_0A}$, and for one slab $C=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d-t+t/K}$.
Half the thickness filled: $C=\dfrac{2KC_0}{K+1}$; as $K\to\infty$ the metal-slab answer returns.
Every patch sees the same $V$ and the same $E=V/d$, but each carries its own charge: $Q_i=\dfrac{K_i\varepsilon_0A_i}{d}\,\Delta V$.
Sums add: $C=\sum\dfrac{K_i\varepsilon_0A_i}{d}$; half the area filled gives $C=C_0\dfrac{K+1}{2}$.

blocks.s: Which case is which? Cut the plates into pieces and you have patches. Cut across the gap and you have layers. Layers add voltages, patches add charges.

blocks.t: ratings and why series is dangerous
lines: Breakdown needs $E_b$, so the safe voltage is $V_{\max}=E_bd$; the best stored density is $\dfrac12\varepsilon_0KE_b^2$. Air: $3\times10^6\ \mathrm{V/m}$, so $0.1\ \mathrm{mm}$ holds about $300\ \mathrm{V}$.
In series, equal charge means $V_i\propto1/C_i$: the smallest capacitor takes the largest voltage and fails first, so a chain is limited by its weakest member.

A $2\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ air capacitor, half the gap filled with $K=4$: layers give $\dfrac{2\cdot4}{5}C_0=1.6C_0$, patches give $\dfrac{4+1}{2}C_0=2.5C_0$. Different answers, same picture - the geometry decides.

blocks.t: Six checks before you hand in

blocks.s: Dimensions: an isolated body has $C\sim\varepsilon_0\times$ length. Limits: $K\to1$ returns vacuum, $b\to\infty$ returns the isolated sphere. Signs: heat cannot be negative, and a dielectric is always pulled toward larger $C$. Endpoints: a transient starts and ends at values the circuit allows. Stability: check curvature when equilibrium is asked. Ratings: compare each local field with $E_b$.

items.cap: Layers share the normal $D$ and add voltages; patches share the voltage and add charges.
Bound charge on the faces opposes the free charge: that is the whole mechanism.

blocks.s: Fixed $Q$ the field falls by $K$; fixed $V$ it does not. Layers add voltages, patches add charges.

sheets.title: RC transients solved, and the capacitor in AC
sheets.sub: One differential equation gives every transient. Two switch rules answer the rest, and one derivative gives the AC response.
sheets.source: Capacitors.md ch.9-10, JEE parts of ch.12

blocks.t: why every answer is an exponential
lines: A cell $E$, resistor $R$, capacitor $C$ in series: $E=Ri+V_C$ with $i=C\dfrac{dV_C}{dt}$, so $RC\dfrac{dV_C}{dt}=E-V_C$.
Separate and integrate: $V_C(t)=E+(V_0-E)e^{-t/RC}$. The approach to the final value is exponential because the drive is proportional to the remaining gap.
Any linear network reduces to this with $V_\infty$ and $R_{\mathrm{th}}$: $V(t)=V_\infty+(V_0-V_\infty)e^{-t/\tau}$, $\tau=R_{\mathrm{th}}C$.
$V_0$: capacitor voltage just before switching - it cannot jump
$V_\infty$: remove the capacitor (open circuit) and solve the resistors
$R_{\mathrm{th}}$: resistance seen from the capacitor terminals, sources killed, dependent sources kept

blocks.s: Clock: one time constant 63 %, two 86 %, three 95 %, five 99.3 %. Inverting: $t=\tau\ln\dfrac{V_\infty-V_0}{V_\infty-V(t)}$.

blocks.t: The two switch rules, and why they hold

lines: Capacitor voltage is the integral of a finite current, so it cannot jump: $V_C(0^+)=V_C(0^-)$. Current can jump, because it is set by the resistors.
So at $t=0^+$: uncharged means a wire, charged means a fixed voltage source. At $t=\infty$ every current has died and the capacitor is an open circuit.
Consequence: a step into a capacitive divider divides by $C$; the final state divides by $R$. That pair of answers is most of what is asked.

blocks.t: discharge, and why energy dies twice as fast
lines: With $E=0$: $V=V_0e^{-t/RC}$ and $i=\dfrac{V_0}{R}e^{-t/RC}$.
Energy $U=\frac12CV^2=\dfrac12CV_0^2e^{-2t/RC}$: the exponent doubles because $U$ goes as $V^2$.
Settling heat between two voltages: $H=\dfrac12C(V_0-V_\infty)^2$, whatever $R$ is - smaller $R$ just means a bigger current for a shorter time.

blocks.s: At DC steady state the capacitor is open, but its voltage need not be zero. Replacing it by a wire is the $t=0^+$ picture, not the final one.

blocks.t: Reservoir capacitor and the AC response

lines: Between recharges the capacitor supplies the load: $Q=I\Delta t$, so $\Delta V\approx\dfrac{I_{\mathrm{load}}\Delta t}{C}$. A $1\ \mathrm{A}$ load fed every $10\ \mathrm{ms}$ with $0.5\ \mathrm{V}$ ripple needs $20\ \mathrm{mF}$.
For $V=V_0\sin\omega t$, $i=C\dfrac{dV}{dt}=\omega CV_0\cos\omega t$: the current leads by $90^\circ$ and its size is $V_0/X_C$ with $X_C=\dfrac{1}{\omega C}$.
Series $RC$: $Z=\sqrt{R^2+X_C^2}$, $\phi=-\arctan(X_C/R)$; at $X_C=R$ the current leads by $45^\circ$.
$2\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ at $10\ \mathrm{V}$ discharged through $1\ \mathrm{M}\Omega$: $\tau=2\ \mathrm{s}$, so at $t=2\ \mathrm{s}$ the voltage is $10e^{-1}=3.68\ \mathrm{V}$.
Energy falls from $100\ \mu\mathrm{J}$ to $13.5\ \mu\mathrm{J}$; the missing $86.5\ \mu\mathrm{J}$ is heat in the resistor.

blocks.t: why a probe loads the circuit
lines: The meter has its own input capacitance $C_m$. Connecting it joins two capacitors, so charge is shared.
A capacitor $C_s$ at $V_0$ then reads $V=V_0\dfrac{C_s}{C_s+C_m}$: with $C_m=C_s$ you lose half the reading. That is why a small capacitor needs a high-impedance probe.

items.cap: Everything except the capacitor is one source plus $R_{\mathrm{th}}$: that is why one exponential is enough.
Voltage rises as $1-e^{-t/\tau}$ while current falls: their areas settle the energy books.

blocks.s: Solve $RC\dot V+V=V_\infty$ once. Then $V_0$, $V_\infty$, $R_{\mathrm{th}}C$ answer every transient.
